problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates **in place** so that each distinct value appears exactly once, keeping the original relative order.

Return the resulting prefix as a list, i.e. the distinct values in order. Your solution should use O(1) extra space beyond the returned list: overwrite the array front-to-back with a write pointer.
hints: Because the array is sorted, equal values are adjacent.
Keep a write index for the next slot of the unique prefix; compare each element with the last value you wrote.
Scan with a read pointer; whenever `nums[read]` differs from `nums[write-1]`, copy it to `nums[write]` and advance write. Return `nums[:write]`.

problems.title: Move Zeroes
problems.description: Given an integer array `nums`, move every `0` to the end of the array while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place with a single pass and without allocating a second array, then return the modified array.
hints: The non-zero elements must keep their order, so you only need to decide where each one goes.
Maintain a write index for the next non-zero slot.
Swap (or copy) each non-zero value to the write index and advance it; the zeros naturally drift to the end.

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` of length `n`, return the value that appears **more than** `n / 2` times. You may assume such a value always exists.

There is a solution that uses only O(1) extra space; try to find it rather than counting everything in a hash map.
constraints: A majority element is guaranteed to exist
hints: If the majority element appears more than half the time, it outnumbers all the other values combined.
Pair off different values: each pair of distinct elements cancels out, and the majority element survives.
Keep a candidate and a counter. If the counter is 0, adopt the current element as candidate; then add 1 if it matches the candidate, otherwise subtract 1.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.description:
An array `nums` holds `n` **distinct** integers, each taken from the range `0..n` inclusive, so exactly one number from that range is absent. Return the missing number.

Try to do it in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
hints: The values come from a fixed range of n+1 numbers and you have n of them.
You know what the total of 0..n should be.
Subtract the sum of the array from n*(n+1)/2, or XOR all indices and values together.

problems.title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
problems.description:
You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n` where every value lies in the range `1..n`, and each value appears **once or twice**. Return all values that appear twice, sorted in ascending order.

A hash set is the easy answer. The interesting version uses O(1) extra space (not counting the output) by exploiting the fact that values double as valid indices.
constraints: Each value appears once or twice
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (plus sorting the output)
hints: Every value is a valid index into the array (after subtracting 1).
Use the sign of `nums[v-1]` as a visited flag for value `v`.
For each element take `v = abs(x)`. If `nums[v-1]` is already negative, `v` is a duplicate; otherwise negate it. Sort the collected duplicates at the end.

problems.title: First Unique Character in a String
problems.description: Given a string `s` of lowercase English letters, return the **index** of the first character that appears exactly once in the whole string. If every character repeats, return `-1`.
hints: You can't decide a character is unique until you've seen the whole string.
Count how many times each letter occurs.
Do a second pass from the left and return the first index whose letter has count 1.

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix
problems.description: Given a list of strings `strs`, return the longest string that is a prefix of **every** string in the list. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string.
problems.complexity: O(total characters) time, O(1) extra space
hints: The common prefix can never be longer than the shortest string.
Compare column by column: character 0 of every word, then character 1, and so on.
Stop at the first column where some word is too short or has a different character; return the prefix up to that column.

problems.title: Isomorphic Strings
problems.description:
Two strings `s` and `t` of equal length are **isomorphic** if the characters of `s` can be replaced one-for-one to produce `t`. Every occurrence of a character must map to the same replacement, the order is preserved, and two different characters of `s` may not map to the same character of `t` (a character may map to itself).

Return `true` if `s` and `t` are isomorphic.
constraints: `s` and `t` consist of printable ASCII characters
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet
hints: Checking only s -> t is not enough; think about 'ab' and 'cc'.
The mapping must be one-to-one, so you need to verify both directions.
Keep two maps (s->t and t->s). For each position, if either map already holds a different partner, return false.

problems.title: Word Pattern
problems.description:
You are given a `pattern` made of lowercase letters and a string `s` of lowercase words separated by single spaces. Return `true` if `s` follows the pattern: there must be a **bijection** between letters of `pattern` and words of `s`, so every letter always stands for the same word and no two letters stand for the same word.

The number of words in `s` must equal the length of `pattern`.
constraints: `s` has lowercase words separated by single spaces, no leading or trailing spaces
problems.complexity: O(n + total characters) time, O(k) space
hints: Split `s` into words first and compare the counts with the pattern length.
A one-way map letter -> word is not enough: 'ab' vs 'dog dog' must fail.
Keep letter -> word and word -> letter maps; any conflict in either direction returns false.

problems.title: Ransom Note
problems.description:
Given two strings `note` and `magazine`, decide whether `note` can be built by cutting individual letters out of `magazine`. Each letter in `magazine` can be used at most once.

Return `true` if it is possible, otherwise `false`.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
problems.complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) space for 26 letters
hints: Order does not matter, only how many of each letter you have.
Count the letters in the magazine.
Walk through `note`, decrementing the count for each letter; if a count would go below zero, return false.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
problems.description: Given a string `s`, return `true` if `s` can become a palindrome after deleting **at most one** character (the deleted character may be anywhere).
hints: Run the usual two-pointer palindrome check from both ends.
At the first mismatch you have exactly one chance: skip the left character or skip the right one.
After the mismatch, check whether `s[l+1..r]` or `s[l..r-1]` is a palindrome with a plain two-pointer helper; no further deletions allowed.

problems.title: Reverse Words in a String
problems.description:
Given a string `s` containing words separated by spaces, return a string with the words in reverse order, joined by exactly one space.

The input may contain leading spaces, trailing spaces, and several consecutive spaces between words. The output must not have any of these: no leading or trailing spaces and a single space between words.
hints: Words are maximal runs of non-space characters.
Extract the words ignoring extra whitespace, then read them back to front.
Split on whitespace (dropping empty pieces), reverse the list and join with a single space. For an O(1)-space follow-up in a mutable array, reverse the whole buffer and then each word.

problems.title: String Compression
problems.description:
Run-length encode the string `s`. Scan left to right and replace every maximal run of the same character with that character followed by the run length. If the run length is `1`, write only the character and **omit** the `1`. Lengths of 10 or more are written with all their digits (e.g. 12 identical letters `a` become `a12`).

Return the encoded string. `s` contains only letters, so digits in the output are never ambiguous.
constraints: `s` consists of upper- and lowercase English letters
hints: Think in terms of runs: where does the current character stop repeating?
Use two indices: `i` marks the start of a run and `j` advances while `s[j] == s[i]`.
Append `s[i]`, and append `str(j - i)` only when the run is longer than 1; then continue from `j`.

problems.title: Merge Sorted Array
problems.description:
You are given two sorted (non-decreasing) integer arrays. `nums1` has length `m + n`: its first `m` entries are the values to merge and the last `n` entries are placeholder zeros that provide room. `nums2` has `n` values.

Merge `nums2` into `nums1` **in place** so that `nums1` becomes one sorted array, and return `nums1`. A solution that needs no extra array fills `nums1` from the back.
hints: Filling from the front would overwrite values of `nums1` you still need.
The largest remaining element must go to the very end, and the end of `nums1` is free space.
Use three pointers: `i = m-1`, `j = n-1`, `k = m+n-1`. Place the larger of `nums1[i]`, `nums2[j]` at `k` and step back. When `j` runs out you are done.

problems.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order.

Sorting the squares works in O(n log n); aim for O(n).
hints: Negative numbers become large positives after squaring, so the largest squares sit at the two ends of the input.
The array is sorted, so the biggest absolute value is at the left or at the right end.
Use two pointers at both ends and fill the output from the back with the larger of the two squares, moving the pointer you used.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Sorted Input
problems.description:
Given a **1-indexed** array `numbers` that is sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer `target`, find two different positions whose values add up to `target`. Return `[i, j]` with `i < j` (1-indexed).

Exactly one valid answer exists. You must use only O(1) extra space, so a hash map is off the table.
hints: The array is sorted: that structure should replace the hash map.
Put one pointer at each end and look at the sum.
If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if it is too large, move the right pointer left; stop when equal.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`, return every **unique** quadruplet `[a, b, c, d]` of values taken from four different indices such that `a + b + c + d == target`.

Each quadruplet must be sorted in ascending order, and the list of quadruplets must itself be sorted lexicographically. No two quadruplets in the answer may be equal as value lists, even if they come from different index choices.

Values can be as large as 10^9 in magnitude, so think about overflow in languages with fixed-width integers.
problems.complexity: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output)
hints: Generalise 3Sum: sort first so duplicates are adjacent and two pointers become possible.
Fix the first two numbers with nested loops, then close in on the remaining pair with a left/right pointer scan.

Skip a value whenever it equals the previous one at the same loop level (for i, for j, and after finding a match for both pointers). That is what prevents duplicate quadruplets. Do not skip before the first candidate at each level.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.description:
An array `nums` contains only the values `0`, `1` and `2` (think red, white, blue). Sort it **in place** so that all `0`s come first, then all `1`s, then all `2`s, and return the array.

Do it in a single pass with O(1) extra space, without calling a library sort and without counting-then-rewriting in two passes.
hints: Three buckets are needed, so one boundary pointer is not enough.
Keep a pointer for where the next 0 goes, another for where the next 2 goes, and a scanning pointer in between.
Dutch national flag: if `nums[mid]` is 0 swap with `low` and advance both; if 2 swap with `high` and decrement only `high` (the swapped-in value is unexamined); if 1 just advance `mid`.

problems.title: Rotate Array
problems.description:
Rotate the array `nums` to the **right** by `k` positions and return the rotated array. Rotating right by 1 moves the last element to the front. `k` can be larger than the length of the array.

A copy-based answer is easy. The interview version asks for O(1) extra space: there is an elegant approach using three in-place reversals.
hints: Rotating by `k` and by `k % n` give the same result.
After a right rotation the last `k` elements end up in front, in their original order.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first `k` elements, then reverse the remaining `n-k` elements.

solutions.python:
def rotate(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    def rev(i, j):
        while i < j:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
            i += 1
            j -= 1
    rev(0, n - 1)
    rev(0, k - 1)
    rev(k, n - 1)
    return nums

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous non-empty subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.

The array may contain negative numbers; if every number is negative the answer is the largest (least negative) single element.
hints: A subarray ending at index i either extends the best one ending at i-1 or starts fresh at i.
Only extend when the running sum so far is positive; a negative prefix can only hurt.
Keep `cur = max(x, cur + x)` and a global `best = max(best, cur)`. Initialise both with `nums[0]`, not 0, so all-negative arrays work.

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous non-empty subarray whose **product** is largest and return that product.

The array can contain negatives and zeros. A single very negative running product can flip into the best product when multiplied by another negative number, and a zero resets everything. The result is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer, and so does every subarray product.
constraints: Every subarray product fits in a 32-bit signed integer
hints: Unlike sums, the smallest (most negative) product so far can become the largest after one more negative factor.
Track both the maximum and the minimum product of a subarray ending at the current index.
For each x, the new max is `max(x, x*prevMax, x*prevMin)` and the new min is `min(x, x*prevMax, x*prevMin)`; update the global answer with the max. A zero naturally resets both.

solutions.python:
def max_product(nums):
    cur_max = cur_min = best = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        a, b = cur_max * x, cur_min * x
        cur_max = max(x, a, b)
        cur_min = min(x, a, b)
        best = max(best, cur_max)
    return best

problems.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by `k`.

The numbers can be negative. Be careful with how your language computes the remainder of a negative number: you need a non-negative remainder in `[0, k)` for the counting trick to work.
hints: A subarray sum equals a difference of two prefix sums.
The difference is divisible by k exactly when the two prefix sums have the same remainder modulo k.

Count how many times each prefix remainder has been seen (start with remainder 0 seen once). For each new prefix remainder r, add `count[r]` to the answer, then increment it. Normalise negatives with `((r % k) + k) % k`.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.description:
Given an array of non-negative integers `nums` and an integer `k >= 1`, return `true` if some subarray of **length at least 2** has a sum that is a multiple of `k`, otherwise `false`. A sum of `0` counts as a multiple of `k`.

The length-two requirement is the part people forget: a single element divisible by `k` does not qualify by itself.
hints: Prefix sums again: a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
Two prefix sums with equal remainder mod k mean the subarray between them is a multiple of k.
Store the **earliest** index for every remainder (remainder 0 at index -1). When you see a remainder again at index i, return true if `i - first >= 2`; do not overwrite the stored index.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.description:
Given an array of **positive** integers `nums` and a positive integer `target`, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is **at least** `target`. If no subarray reaches the target, return `0`.

Because every element is positive, the sum only grows when you extend a window and only shrinks when you drop elements; use that to get O(n).
hints: Positivity means adding elements always increases the sum.
Grow the right end of a window until the sum reaches the target, then try to shrink from the left while it still does.
Track the smallest window length seen while the sum is >= target; if it never updates, return 0.

problems.title: Max Consecutive Ones III
problems.description:
Given a binary array `nums` and an integer `k`, you may flip at most `k` zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive `1`s you can obtain.

Phrase it differently and it becomes a classic window question: what is the longest subarray that contains at most `k` zeros?
constraints: 0 <= k <= nums.length (k may exceed the number of zeros)
hints: You do not need to actually flip anything; count zeros inside a window.
A window is valid while it contains at most k zeros.
Expand the right pointer; if the zero count exceeds k, advance the left pointer until it is valid again. Track the maximum window size.

problems.title: Fruit Into Baskets
problems.description:
A row of trees is described by the array `fruits`, where `fruits[i]` is the type of fruit on tree `i`. You carry exactly two baskets and each basket holds a single fruit type (unlimited quantity). Starting at any tree, you walk right and must pick exactly one fruit from every tree you pass, stopping at the first tree whose fruit does not fit in either basket.

Return the maximum number of fruits you can pick, which is the length of the longest contiguous stretch with at most two distinct types.
constraints: 0 <= fruits[i] < fruits.length (the tests use small non-negative integers)
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (at most 3 keys in the map)
hints: Reword it: longest subarray with at most two distinct values.
Maintain a frequency map of the current window; its size is the number of distinct types.
When the map grows to three types, shrink from the left, decrementing counts and deleting keys that reach zero, until only two remain.

problems.title: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
problems.description:
Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, return the length of the longest substring of `s` that contains **at most** `k` distinct characters.

If `k` is `0` the answer is `0`. Your solution should be linear: when the window becomes invalid you must shrink it correctly, remembering that a character only leaves the distinct set when its **last** occurrence in the window is dropped.
hints: Think of a window [left, right] and a frequency map of the characters in it.
The window is valid while the map has at most k keys. Grow right one character at a time.
When the map has more than k keys, move left forward: decrement the count of `s[left]` and delete the key only when its count hits zero. Update the best length after the window is valid again.

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.description:
Given two strings `s` and `p`, return the starting indices (in ascending order) of every substring of `s` that is an anagram of `p`, i.e. a rearrangement of exactly the letters of `p`. Overlapping matches are all reported.

If `p` is longer than `s`, the answer is an empty list.
constraints: `s` and `p` consist of lowercase English letters
hints: An anagram has the same length and the same letter counts as `p`.
Slide a fixed-size window of length `len(p)` over `s`, updating counts incrementally instead of recounting.

Keep a count difference per letter plus a counter of letters that are not balanced (or compare two 26-length arrays). Add the entering letter, remove the leaving one, and record the index when everything matches.

problems.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
problems.description:
You are given an integer array `nums` that never changes and a list of `queries`, where each query `[l, r]` asks for the sum of `nums[l..r]` inclusive. Return a list with the answer to every query, in order.

A loop per query is O(n) each. With many queries, preprocess once so that every query is O(1).
constraints: 0 <= l <= r < nums.length for every query
hints: Many queries over the same array: do the work once up front.
A range sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
Build `prefix` where `prefix[i]` is the sum of the first `i` elements. Then `sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]`.

problems.title: Find Pivot Index
problems.description:
The **pivot index** of an integer array `nums` is an index where the sum of all elements strictly to its left equals the sum of all elements strictly to its right. The element at the pivot itself is in neither sum, and the sum of an empty side is `0`.

Return the **leftmost** pivot index, or `-1` if none exists.
hints: Left sum == right sum is the same as left == total - left - nums[i].
Compute the total once, then sweep from the left keeping a running left sum.
At each index check `left == total - left - nums[i]`; if so return i, otherwise add `nums[i]` to `left`. The first match is the leftmost one, and index 0 or n-1 can pivot because an empty side is 0.
